description: On the night of **November 9 to 10, 1989**, Berliners tore down with their bare hands the wall that had divided their city for **28 years**. A misunderstanding on live television sped up the end of the Cold War.

hero.hook: The most closely watched wall in the world fell after one sentence slipped out on television.

blocks.text: On the night of **November 9 to 10, 1989**, Berliners from East and West went at the wall that had cut their city apart for **28 years**. The moment marked the symbolic collapse of the [[iron curtain]], the border that split Europe in two.
It was not just a street party. It was the result of a socialist economy out of breath, a new Soviet line, and a botched press conference that opened the borders too early.

After 1945, Berlin was cut into zones. Between **1949** and **1961**, more than **3 million** people left the [[GDR]], the German Democratic Republic (East Germany), for the West through Berlin. Many of them were young and highly trained. To stop the bleeding, barbed wire went up on the night of **August 12 to 13, 1961**, and then a wall **155 km** long.

blocks.caption: The fall of the Berlin Wall, November 1989

blocks.text: The East German regime officially called it the “Anti-Fascist Protective Rampart,” claiming it kept spies out rather than kept its own citizens in.
Watchtowers, mines, dogs: **138** people were killed trying to cross. West Berlin became a capitalist showcase locked inside hostile territory. The wall was the concrete face of the Cold War.

sections.title: A wall to stop a people

blocks.text: Under **Mikhail Gorbachev**, the Soviet leader, the USSR refused to crush its satellites the way it had in 1968, during [[The Prague Spring (August 1968)]]. The reforms known as [[Glasnost and Perestroika]], openness and restructuring, shook the whole bloc. In May **1989**, Hungary opened its border with Austria: the first real breach in the iron curtain.

In Leipzig, the Monday marches chanted “Wir sind das Volk” (“We are the people”). [[Erich Honecker]], the East German leader, who had promised the wall would stand “another 50 or 100 years,” was replaced in October. Too late: the movement could no longer be stopped.

On **November 9**, the spokesman **Günter Schabowski** read out on live television a note he had not had time to study. Asked when the new travel rules applied, he said: “Immediately, without delay.” In fact they were meant to start the next day.

blocks.caption: Crowds in West Berlin on the night of November 9, 1989

blocks.text: In **1988**, Bruce Springsteen played East Berlin in front of **300,000** people. Many see that concert as a wake-up moment for young East Germans.

Berliners rushed to the checkpoints, the border crossings. The guards, with no orders, finally opened them. Around 11:30 p.m., at Bornholmer Strasse, the barriers gave way. German unity was decided in the street.

Driven by **Helmut Kohl**, the West German chancellor, Germany was reunified on **October 3, 1990**. The shock carried away Poland, Czechoslovakia (the [[Velvet Revolution]]), Bulgaria, and Romania. The USSR itself disappeared in December **1991**.

events.detail: East Berlin locked itself down to stop the exodus.
events.title: The wall goes up

events.detail: A communication blunder, and the checkpoints opened.
events.title: The wall falls

blocks.text: The fall of the wall (**November 9, 1989**), set off by a communication blunder, opened the way to German reunification and sped up the collapse of the Soviet bloc.

sections.title: From Berlin to the end of a world
